channel.title: Said & Checked: Congress and Government Spending — AskAmerica
channel.description: What officeholders said each day about Congress and Government Spending, and which statements government data supports, contradicts or rules out.

item.title: Said & Checked, Congress and Government Spending, 2026-11-20: 3 contradicted (Steny Hoyer, David Schweikert, Chip Roy)
item.description:
False or contradicted

  • Steny Hoyer, U.S. Representative: “The decade between fiscal year 2001 and fiscal year 2010, we averaged 108 days a year under continuing resolutions.” Contradicted. CRS R42647's Table 3 gives total days under continuing resolutions for fiscal 2001-2010 of 82, 102, 143, 123, 69, 92, 365, 92, 162 and 79, an average of about 131 days a year, not 108; leaving out fiscal 2007's full-year resolution gives about 105. What remains open is whether the figure comes from a different counting method.
  • David Schweikert, U.S. Representative: “OMB underestimated the 2026 deficits by--so this is OMB--$391 billion.” Contradicted. OMB's FY2026 Mid-Session Review projected a fiscal 2026 deficit of $2.220 trillion, while AskAmerica's Treasury data show the actual deficit was $1.993 trillion ($7.396 trillion in outlays less $5.403 trillion in receipts), so that projection overstated the deficit by about $228 billion. OMB's earlier budget-proposal projection was not located, so whether it understated the deficit remains open.
  • Chip Roy, U.S. Representative: “The empire is that which gave us the $42 trillion of debt” Contradicted. Treasury's Debt to the Penny series in AskAmerica's warehouse shows total public debt of $40.715 trillion on Nov. 17, 2026, about $1.3 trillion below $42 trillion. The Treasury source could not be read directly outside the warehouse.

Disagreements

  • David Schweikert, U.S. Representative: “The total debt is--and I think this chart is from yesterday--$40.662 trillion.” (supported)
    Chip Roy, U.S. Representative: “The empire is that which gave us the $42 trillion of debt” (contradicted)
    Both statements in context

item.title: Said & Checked, Congress and Government Spending, 2026-11-19: none false or contradicted, 1 unsettled (Mike Lawler)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Mike Lawler, U.S. Representative from New York: “they shut the government down for 118 days with respect to the Department of Homeland Security.” Unsettled. As reported by NPR, the House passed the bill ending the DHS shutdown on its 76th day, April 30, 2026, but that bill left out ICE and Customs and Border Protection, whose funding was moved to a separate reconciliation bill whose outcome was not found, so a longer count for part of the department cannot be ruled out. The appropriations record itself could not be read directly.

item.title: Said & Checked, Congress and Government Spending, 2026-11-18: 1 contradicted (Darrell Issa)
item.description:
False or contradicted

  • Darrell Issa, U.S. Representative from California: “Currently the Bureau of Land Management spends a not insignificant number of dollars every year and growing maintaining 847 acres of land that earns no money” Contradicted. The text of H.R. 8483 in the Congressional Record divides the approximately 847 acres into about 164 acres of Bureau of Land Management land ('Parcel 1') and about 683 acres of Forest Service land ('Parcels 2 and 3'), so BLM does not manage all 847 acres. The total acreage matches. The record gives no revenue or maintenance-cost figures, so 'earns no money' was not tested.

item.title: Said & Checked, Congress and Government Spending, 2026-11-17: none false or contradicted, 4 unsettled (Chuck Grassley)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Chuck Grassley, U.S. Senator from Iowa: “Over the six decades spanning since the end of World War II, the deficit never once exceeded 6 percent of GDP.” Unsettled. In OMB's historical table (read from a secondary copy) the largest deficit from 1947 through 2008 was 5.9 percent of GDP, in 1983, but fiscal 1946 was 7.0 percent. The statement holds if the six decades start in 1947 and not if they start in 1946.
  • Chuck Grassley, U.S. Senator from Iowa: “They have fanned inflation, driving up the cost of living.” Unsettled. A Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco analysis estimates that pandemic fiscal support raised inflation by about 3 percentage points by the end of 2021, with considerable uncertainty; other studies attribute smaller shares or point to supply factors. The evidence concerns pandemic spending rather than persistent deficits and turns on model assumptions.
  • Chuck Grassley, U.S. Senator from Iowa: “In 2026, interest rates on the national debt totaled $1.14 trillion, up 11 percent over last year.” Unsettled. American Action Forum, citing CBO, reports net interest up $115 billion, 11 percent, in fiscal 2026, consistent with $1.14 trillion. AskAmerica's Treasury data show the narrower Monthly Treasury Statement 'Net Interest' line at $1.052 trillion, up 8.4 percent from $0.970 trillion; CBO's own figure could not be read directly, so which measure is meant decides it.

item.title: Said & Checked, Congress and Government Spending, 2026-11-15: none false or contradicted, 4 unsettled (Bill Cassidy)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Bill Cassidy, U.S. Senator from Louisiana: “I had a commitment from both Thune and from Mike Ccrepo to have a hearing and a markup on a Social Security bill.” Unsettled. AskAmerica's bill records show the senator's S. 4979, the PROMISE Act of 2026, referred to the Finance Committee on July 14, 2026, with no markup recorded. Raw Story reported in August that the Finance chairman was among senators he met on the bill; it records no public commitment by either senator to a hearing and markup.
  • Bill Cassidy, U.S. Senator from Louisiana: “And the president actually has given me personal commitment that he would support it and his administration has been very helpful.” Unsettled. Raw Story reported in August 2026 that a White House spokesperson declined to comment on the bill and that the president has vowed not to touch Social Security. That is neither public support nor public opposition, and no White House statement on the bill was found.
  • Bill Cassidy, U.S. Senator from Louisiana: “we borrow $1.5 trillion, we put it in investment funds separate from Social Security trust fund, put it into the broader economy, and allow it to grow over six decades, at which point it paid for up to 70 percent…” Unsettled. An analysis by Boston College's Center for Retirement Research describes the plan as $1.5 trillion borrowed and held in a fund separate from the Social Security trust fund, which matches. The 70 percent figure is the senator's own estimate and no bill text or actuarial score was found; the Boston College simulation finds the fund repaying about 60 percent of the total borrowing at the median, on its own assumptions.
